bayesfoRest: Forest Plots for Bayesian Meta Analyses in R

Overview

bayesfoRest is an R package for creating publication-ready forest plots from Bayesian meta-analyses. It provides a comprehensive solution for visualizing meta-analytic results with support for various effect measures, subgroup analyses, and risk of bias assessments.

Key Features

  • Bayesian Forest Plots: Create forest plots from models fitted with brms, bayesma, bayesmeta, MetaStan, rstanarm, rstan, cmdstanr, RoBMA or R2jags
  • Multiple Effect Measures: Support for OR, HR, RR, IRR, MD, and SMD
  • Density or Boxplot Output: Show study posteriors as densities or horizontal boxplots
  • Subgroup Analysis: Built-in support for subgroup meta-analyses
  • Risk of Bias Integration: Incorporate risk of bias assessments (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, ROBINS-E, QUADAS-2, CLARITY, ROB-NMA, PROBAST)
  • Shrinkage Visualisation: Display shrinkage effects with density plots or point intervals
  • ROPE Support: Add a Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE) to plots
  • Extensive Customisation: Colours, fonts, labels, and layout
  • Overall Plot: Combined visualisation of the pooled effect, prediction and heterogeneity posterior distributions
  • Sensitivity Plot: Create visualisations of different priors and model types, with probabilities of benefit/harm
  • ECDF Model Plot: Plot comparing posterior distributions across different model strategies (e.g., random effects, comon-effect) under a single prior specification.
  • ECDF Prior Plot: Plot comparing posterior distributions across different prior specifications for a single model type.
  • Risk of Bias Plots: Traffic light plot or weighted bar chart of judgements per domain, standalone or weighted by study
  • Funnel Plot: Study-level effect sizes plotted against precision.

Installation

You can install the development version of bayesfoRest from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("BLMoran/bayesfoRest")

Basic Usage

The examples below use the binary_outcome dataset that comes with the package. First prepare the effect sizes with metafor and fit a Bayesian model (bayesma, RoBMA, bayesmeta, MetaStan; brms is shown here):

library(bayesfoRest)
library(metafor)
library(brms)

binary_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = Event_Intervention, bi = Outcome_Intervention_No,
  ci = Event_Control, di = Outcome_Control_No,
  n1i = N_Intervention, n2i = N_Control,
  data = binary_outcome) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sei = sqrt(vi))

model_bin <- brm(
  yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | Author),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = binary_es,
  prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept) +
          prior(cauchy(0, 0.5), class = sd),
  iter = 4000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))

Binary Outcome Forest Plot (Odds Ratio)

Assign the model object, data frame, and measure, then the study-level arguments as unquoted column names, within bayes_forest():

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

For continuous outcomes, use mean_ctrl, mean_int, sd_ctrl and sd_int instead of the event columns. For time-to-event and rate outcomes, use time_ctrl and time_int.

Common-Effect Meta-Analysis

For a fixed/common-effect analysis, fit a model without a study-level random effect (drop (1 | Author) in brms). bayes_forest() auto-detects the pooling type from the model, so no shrinkage or heterogeneity (tau) panel is drawn, and prediction intervals are unavailable (there’s no tau to predict a new study from).

model_bin_ce <- brm(
  yi | se(sei) ~ 1,
  family = gaussian(),
  data = binary_es,
  prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept),
  iter = 4000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin_ce,
  model_type = "common_effect",
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Boxplot Output

plot_output = "boxplot" draws each study as a horizontal boxplot. Shrinkage estimates are shown as point intervals.

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  plot_output = "boxplot",
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Add Subgroups 

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  subgroup = TRUE,
  subgroupvar = Subgroup,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Add Risk of Bias Columns 

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  subgroup = TRUE,
  subgroupvar = Subgroup,
  add_rob = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Add Risk of Bias Legend 

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  subgroup = TRUE,
  subgroupvar = Subgroup,
  add_rob = TRUE,
  add_rob_legend = TRUE,
  rob_tool = "rob2",
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Exclude Studies with High Risk of Bias 

bayes_forest(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  subgroup = TRUE,
  subgroupvar = Subgroup,
  add_rob = TRUE,
  add_rob_legend = TRUE,
  rob_tool = "rob2",
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Standalone Risk of Bias Plot 

rob_plot(
  data = binary_outcome,
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  rob_tool = "rob2",
  add_rob_legend = TRUE
)

If your data has domain judgements but no overall column, bayes_forest() and rob_plot() derive one automatically using the tool’s rules.

Risk of Bias Summary Plot

rob_summary() shows the weighted proportion of studies at each judgement, per domain, as a stacked bar chart.

rob_summary(
  data = binary_outcome,
  rob_tool = "rob2",
  title = "Risk of Bias Summary"
)

Overall Plot 

overall_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  add_tau = TRUE,
  add_pred = TRUE,
  incl_mu_prior = TRUE,
  incl_tau_prior = TRUE,
  add_null_range = TRUE,
  mu_xlim = c(0.1, 3.5),
  tau_xlim = c(0, 1.5),
  plot_arrangement = "vertical"
)

The dashed lines are the priors, drawn on the same density scale as the posteriors. They are read from brms and bayesmeta models; for other backends, pass them with mu_prior and tau_prior (e.g. mu_prior = bf_normal(0, 1)). With add_null_range = TRUE the shaded region defaults to an odds ratio of 0.9 to 1.1; set your own with null_range.

Funnel Plot 

funnel_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  yi_col = "yi",
  sei_col = "sei",
  label_studies = TRUE
)

Sensitivity Plot

Priors are written with the bf_*() helpers, so the same list works whichever backend the model was fitted with. For the pooled effect use bf_normal() or bf_student_t(). For the heterogeneity use bf_half_normal(), bf_half_cauchy(), bf_half_t(), bf_exponential(), bf_lognormal() or bf_uniform(), or the empirical priors bf_turner() (binary outcomes) and bf_rhodes() (continuous outcomes), which are informative and especially useful when there are few studies. If the model’s backend cannot fit a prior exactly, you get an error rather than a substitute; ?bf_priors lists which backends support which priors.

priors <- list(
  vague = list(
    name = "Vague",
    mu_prior = bf_normal(0, 10),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 1)),
  weakreg = list(
    name = "Weakly Regularising",
    mu_prior = bf_normal(0, 1),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 0.5)),
  informative = list(
    name = "Informative",
    mu_prior = bf_normal(0, 0.5),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 0.3))
)

sensitivity_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors,
  measure = "OR",
  rob_var = Overall,
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  incl_common_effect = TRUE,
  add_probs = FALSE,
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5),
  add_null_range = TRUE
)

Sensitivity Plot with Probabilities 

sensitivity_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors,
  measure = "OR",
  rob_var = Overall,
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  incl_common_effect = TRUE,
  add_probs = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5),
  add_null_range = TRUE
)

Publication-bias-adjusted models come from a RoBMA fit: pass it with robma_fit = your_robma_fit and choose the components with incl_robma, incl_pet_peese and incl_selection_weight.

ECDF Plots

ecdf_model_plot() compares the posterior of the pooled effect across models for one prior set:

ecdf_model_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors["weakreg"],
  measure = "OR",
  rob_var = Overall,
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  incl_common_effect = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5),
  add_null_range = TRUE
)

ecdf_prior_plot() compares it across prior sets for one model:

ecdf_prior_plot(
  model = model_bin,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors,
  measure = "OR",
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5),
  add_null_range = TRUE
)

Dependencies

bayesfoRest depends on several R packages:

  • metafor for meta-analysis preparation (suggested)
  • brms, bayesmeta, MetaStan, RoBMA, bayesma and other backends for Bayesian model fitting (suggested; install the ones you use)
  • gt for creating tables
  • patchwork for combining plots
  • ggplot2 for plotting
  • ggdist for density plotting
  • tidybayes for tidy workflow
  • dplyr, tidyr, purrr for data manipulation
  • paletteer for colour palettes
  • fontawesome for risk of bias icons
  • posterior for working with posterior draws
